summary.text: Ocean heat is tracked through seawater temperature at every depth, and experts use those readings to work out how much heat the ocean holds.
Seawater temperature shifts with depth, place and season, and it matters for the global climate, ocean currents and marine habitats.
The oceans are warming because of climate change, fastest above 700 m, and in 2022 the global ocean was the hottest ever recorded.

items.prompt: A warm surface current flows out of the tropics toward the poles and loses its warmth along the way. What happens to that water?

options.label: It grows lighter and spreads out
It turns straight into sea ice

items.explain: As the current cools away from the tropics the water becomes denser and sinks, later flowing back toward the equator as a deep current.

items.prompt: If you scooped a bucket of seawater from a random spot anywhere in the ocean's full volume, what temperature would it most likely be?
items.explain: Cold deep water makes up about 90% of the ocean's volume and sits at a very uniform 0-3 °C.

items.prompt: A report says 'the sea there was 22 °C' but never says how far below the surface the reading was taken. Why is that a problem?

options.label: Thermometers only work at the surface
Temperature can change a lot with depth
Seawater is the same temperature everywhere
Only salinity changes below the surface

items.explain: Below the surface the depth of a reading matters because temperature can vary a lot with depth, especially during the day.

items.prompt: On a calm, very sunny afternoon at sea, what tends to happen in the top part of the water?

options.label: Ice crystals form at the surface
Wind mixes it to one even temperature
Cold deep water rises to the top
A warm layer forms over cooler water

items.explain: Low wind and strong sunshine can build a warm surface layer with a sharp drop in temperature beneath it, called a diurnal thermocline.

items.prompt: Compared with warm surface water, how salty is the cold surface water in polar regions usually?
items.explain: Warm surface water is generally saltier than polar water, whose upper layers are cold and fresh.

items.prompt: Climate change is adding heat to the oceans. Which part of the ocean is warming fastest?

options.label: No part; only the air is warming

items.explain: The upper ocean above 700 m is warming fastest, though the warming trend reaches throughout the ocean.
